In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate. Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds. I pray for blessing and peace upon him who was sent as a mercy to the worlds, and upon his family and his Companions and whoever is guided by his guidance and takes his sunnah as his way until the Day of Judgement.

To proceed: God created the human being with an innate love of might and honour (ʿizzah), so that he strives to attain it by every path and by every means. But this might has causes that lead to it, and it is not attained without them. Many people look for it in the wrong place and seek it where it is not to be sought.

The great mass of those who seek might seek it through the affairs of this perishing world — through the authority and the instruments of overwhelming power in it, and likewise through the sovereignty and abundance and wealth and other things in it. None of these are causes of might. God, exalted be He, made that clear in His Book in an explicit text, saying: {Do they seek might with them? Truly might belongs entirely to God} (Sūrat al-Nisāʾ 4:139).

So all might belongs to God, glorified and exalted; and the created being attains might only by connection with the Creator, glorified and exalted, and by depending upon Him and relying upon Him alone. For this reason God, exalted be He, said: {And to God belongs might, and to His Messenger and to the believers; but the hypocrites do not understand} (Sūrat al-Munāfiqūn 63:8).

The hypocrites used to suppose that the poor among the Emigrants — who had no homeland and no wealth and were not in their own dwellings, and whom the dearest and nearest of people to them had driven out — had no claim upon might. For that reason they said, on the campaign of the Banu al-Mustaliq: {If we return to Medina, the mightier will surely drive out the more abased from it} (Sūrat al-Munāfiqūn 63:8).

So they supposed that these poor ones, whom God praised for their poverty and commended in His Book on account of it, had no refuge and no might, and that they could only be driven out of this city by the might of the hypocrites, who had wealth and children and social standing.

But God, glorified and exalted, dispelled this opinion and refuted those who advanced it and annulled it entirely. For the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, was one of the Emigrants; and God gave him the choice between being a prophet-king and being a prophet-servant, and he chose to be a prophet-servant. He used to dwell in a chamber such that if a man stood up his hand would touch its roof; and he would sleep on a reed mat that left its mark in his side — may my father and mother be his ransom, God bless him and grant him peace — so that when he awoke the mark of the fronds was in his ribs. And three months would pass in succession in which no fire was kindled in his houses. And all the people of the earth gathered in enmity against him, and God turned their scheming back into their own throats and they attained nothing of him; while he attained what God had written for him and what He had undertaken to him of victory and establishment.

The opinion of the hypocrites is a refuted opinion, but they expressed it on several occasions. On the day of the Confederates, when the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, and the believers were besieged between the two lava-fields of Medina — and they were a small number, not exceeding one thousand five hundred men, and they had no external support, and the unbelievers of the people of the Arabian Peninsula among those who associate partners with God came upon them from above them, and the Jews came from below them — God described that situation with a tremendous description, saying: {When they came upon you from above you and from below you, and when the eyes swerved and the hearts reached the throats, and you thought thoughts about God; there the believers were tested and shaken with a severe shaking} (Sūrat al-Aḥzāb 33:10–11).

The hypocrites expressed their view of this situation and said, as God related of them: {When the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease say: God and His Messenger promised us nothing but delusion} (Sūrat al-Aḥzāb 33:12). They said: "Muhammad claims that the treasures of Chosroes and Caesar will be opened to you — and here you are today, not one of you able to go out to relieve himself."

And six years had not passed before God opened the treasures of Chosroes and Caesar to those poor ones besieged in Medina, and they were spent in the path of God. So it was known that the claim of the hypocrites was refuted and false, and that what they expected — that the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions would never return and would never have any state in this earth — was the false claim and the evil thought.

They expressed that also on another occasion, when the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, went out to raid the Jews at Khaybar. The Jews had gathered all their forces, and the idolaters of the Arabs and the Christians of Syria supported them, and there was gathered for them of wealth and horses and weapons more than they had expected, and they filled their fortresses with kinds of provisions and merchandise. And the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, went out to them raiding with one thousand five hundred fighters, riding a donkey.

So the hypocrites said: "Do you suppose that Muhammad will return to you? By God, he will not return to you after this year of his, and the Jews will surely kill them as Ad and Iram were killed." So God, exalted be He, sent down upon the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, in Sūrat al-Fatḥ: {And that He may punish the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women and the men and women who associate partners with God, who think evil thoughts about God. Upon them is the turn of evil} (Sūrat al-Fatḥ 48:6). And God made this thought clear in what He related of them in His words: {Rather, you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families, and that was made pleasing in your hearts, and you thought evil thoughts, and you were a ruined people} (Sūrat al-Fatḥ 48:12).

God has written might for all His messengers, and He followed after them with Muhammad, God bless him and grant him peace, and wrote might for him and wrote abasement and lowliness for everyone who opposed his command; and He helped him with awe cast a month's journey ahead, and left that help to his followers.

This might which people seek and look for is sought only by lowering oneself before God, glorified and exalted, and submitting before Him, and by performing His worship in accordance with what He laid down, and by following His noble Messenger, God bless him and grant him peace, in everything he brought.

For that reason there is no doubt that God, glorified and exalted, has written acceptance among people for those poor and destitute ones who owned nothing and had no helper. The believers in the easts of the earth and its wests today — any one of them would wish to see a garment that Bilal ibn Rabah wore, or Ammar ibn Yasir; merely by seeing something that touched those pure bodies the believers rejoice, because God has written in their hearts love for those who helped God and His Messenger, for whom God appointed the abiding, everlasting might.

And what you witness in your hearts of love for those few is worth nothing of what God has prepared for them of might in the abode of the hereafter. For they were mentioned in the highest assembly before they were mentioned in the lower assembly. It is established as sound (ṣaḥīḥ) from the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, that he said: "When God loves a servant, He calls to Gabriel: I love so-and-so, so love him — and Gabriel loves him. Then Gabriel calls out concerning him among the people of heaven: God loves so-and-so, so love him — and the people of heaven love him. Then acceptance is placed for him in the earth."

This might which we witness in our hearts towards those few who sacrificed and gave in the path of God — even if their sacrifice were small and slight — cannot be compared with anything that comes after. For the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Do not revile my Companions. For if one of you were to spend the like of the mountain of Uhud in gold, it would not reach the mudd of one of them, nor half of it."

A mere mudd of barley spent by one of those poor ones who were driven from their homes and their properties in the path of God and in support of His Messenger, God bless him and grant him peace — if one of those who come after them were to spend the like of the mountain of Uhud in gold, it would not reach that mudd in the sight of God. For God's scale is not like the scales of the people of this world, who look at perishing material things and look at usefulness and profit — as one of the hypocrites said: "What does this man's mudd avail God and His Messenger?" — when a man of the Ansar came who owned nothing but a mudd of barley, carrying it in the corner of his garment, and the hypocrites said: "What does this man's mudd avail God and His Messenger?"

God, glorified and exalted, is the Self-Sufficient; and when He commands His servants to spend, that is only so that they may send forward for themselves. He is the One who multiplies for whomever He wills; and He set out a remarkable parable of multiplication, in a single grain sown in the earth, from which there comes an ear, in every ear seven hundred grains, and the ears increase until they reach seven hundred ears, and so on. This multiplication is only an example by which God's multiplication of the deeds of those whose service and worship He has approved may be understood.

God, glorified and exalted, has no need of anything His servants offer: {Neither their flesh nor their blood reaches God, but God-consciousness from you reaches Him} (Sūrat al-Ḥajj 22:37). So everything the servants offer of acts of obedience — God has no need of it in anything of His victory, for He said in His Book: {That is so; and had God willed He would have taken vengeance upon them Himself, but that He may test some of you by means of others} (Sūrat Muḥammad 47:4).

For this reason people are not rewarded in proportion to usefulness and exertion, but rather in proportion to what has settled in the hearts of faith and what has become firm in them of God-consciousness. The most blessed campaign and the most far-reaching in effect is the campaign of al-Hudaybiyah, in which no fighting occurred and no great wealth was spent and no one was martyred in the path of God. But God knew from the hearts of the Companions of Muhammad, God bless him and grant him peace, truthfulness and God-consciousness, so He sent down upon them His greatest good pleasure, after which there is no anger. So they walk upon the earth with their sins forgiven; their sins do not occur except forgiven. And no one who pledged allegiance beneath the tree will enter the Fire.

For that reason He said: {God was indeed pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you beneath the tree, and He knew what was in their hearts, so He sent down tranquillity upon them and rewarded them with a near victory and many spoils that they would take; and God is ever Mighty, Wise} (Sūrat al-Fatḥ 48:18–19).

Those people — God knew from their hearts truthfulness and sincerity, so He hastened to them His greatest good pleasure, after which there is no anger, and hastened to them the opening and the establishment; because they traded with God, mighty and majestic, and God made their bargain profitable.

When the pledge was finished, Jabir said: The Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, looked at us and said: "You are the best of the people of the earth." And he said, God bless him and grant him peace: "By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, no one who pledged allegiance beneath the tree will enter the Fire."

So they lived with this might. Whoever of them lived upon the earth walked on his two feet knowing that he was of the people of the Garden, and knowing that he was not veiled from God — even if he committed fornication, even if he stole, even if he drank wine, his sin would not occur except forgiven. It is the might above which there is no might.

Those people realised that what people compete over of the affairs of this world is perishing and has no permanence. For that reason they pledged allegiance unto death. They knew that what deserves to be competed for is the everlasting, the abiding, that has no cutting off.

If a person attained the sovereignty of Shaddad ibn Ad over this earth and lived as long as Noah lived upon it, his end must inevitably be to vanish. And likewise, if his remaining were decreed for a long period, like Iblis, he would inevitably grow weary of remaining. For this world is a thing one wearies of, and everything in it of pleasures is cut off. But as for the bliss of the Garden, it does not vanish and is not cut off, and one does not weary of anything in it: {Whenever they are provided with a fruit from it as provision, they say: This is what we were provided with before — and they are given it in resemblance} (Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:25). So they do not weary of anything in it in any way whatever, and nothing of its pleasures is cut off. The first pleasure a person attains, when something of its ease and fragrance reaches him, continues, even if after it there come billions of pleasures, each pleasure remaining following upon the other without interruption; so nothing of its bliss is cut off.

Those people, when they affirmed the truth of this and their hearts drank it in, and God wrote faith in their hearts, knew that what people compete over is worth nothing, and that those who occupy themselves with it are occupying themselves with perishing trivialities; and they saw them according to the measure of their aspirations. For whoever's concern is confined to this worldly life and its perishing adornments — his aspiration is low and weak; he is concerned only with the wearisome, vanishing bottom.

For that reason, if a person wishes to know the value of what people compete over in this world, let him look at the rubbish heaps: he will find there specimens of everything people compete over. People compete over towering buildings — and they will be demolished after a few years, and you will find their rubble in the rubbish heaps. They compete over beautiful clothes and soft furnishings — and you will find their remains thrown in the rubbish heaps. They compete over foods and drinks and other things — and you will find their traces thrown in the rubbish heaps. They compete over cars or aircraft or other things — and you will find their remains thrown in the rubbish heaps.

This world is all like this. It is established as sound from the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, that he said: "It was binding upon God that He should raise nothing of this world but that He brings it low."

For this we have needed to review a little this foundation among the foundations of conception: the foundation of what might is sought as — from where is it sought, and what is the means of reaching it?

The first thing a person ought to conceive is that he is a servant owned by God, and that he is an employee on a defined assignment, and that over him is a supervision that nothing escapes — he cannot hide any of his own affairs from God — and that he has a fixed term and a fixed time, and if he does not perform the assignment within it he can never make it up.

If a person knows this, he knows that he did not come to this worldly life to live for ever and eternally, nor did he come to it to remain for endless ages, nor did he come to it for it to be his abiding abode. He came to it only to make of it a provision by which he provisions himself on his journey to the abode of the hereafter. From here he will be eager for what is there and for what lies before him, and will treat this world as he treats a tree beneath which he takes his midday rest, waiting for the sun to decline so that he may go out on his long journey.

The Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, said: "What have I to do with this world? I am only like a rider who took shade beneath a tree." So this world is like the shade of a tree, under which a person shelters to protect himself from the heat of the noon — but he is a traveller and cannot lean upon it and settle in it; rather he must cover the distance in the appointed time.

Whoever wants might must free himself from all other things and be a servant purely to God. So long as a person finds in himself a leaning and an inclination and a love for something of this world — an unnatural love, meaning a love that requires the overriding of all convictions and conceptions — let him know that he cannot attain might by that; rather he is still a slave, abased to something of this perishing world. And so long as he responds to the pressures in this life, and the blame of a blamer concerning God touches him — he fears someone other than God, he remembers that a punishment will fall upon him from someone other than God — he does not attain this might.

Do you not see the mighty stand which Abraham took, when all the people of the earth schemed against him, foremost among them his father and his uncles and his relatives? God inspired him with the argument against them and made him prevail: {And that was Our argument which We gave to Abraham against his people. We raise in degrees whomever We will. Truly your Lord is Wise, Knowing} (Sūrat al-Anʿām 6:83).

For when they disputed with him they said to him: "We own everything, and we shall kindle the fire for you and cast you into it, and you will not affect anything of our affairs and will not change anything of our convictions." And what was Abraham's answer? {He said: Do you dispute with me concerning God, when He has guided me? And I do not fear what you associate with Him, except that my Lord should will something. My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge. Will you not then remember? And how should I fear what you have associated, while you do not fear that you have associated with God that for which He has sent down upon you no authority? Which of the two parties has better right to security, if you know? Those who believe and do not clothe their faith in wrongdoing — for them is security, and they are the rightly guided} (Sūrat al-Anʿām 6:80–82).

It is the far-reaching argument with which God inspired him, and which cut off from those people everything they were clamouring with of arguments and everything they were considering of their instruments and their material power. For Abraham mentioned to them his relationship with God and his reliance upon Him.

This might also appeared in another manifestation in the case of Moses, peace be upon him, when he went out with the Children of Israel, travelling with them by night in emigration in the path of God. Then when the dawn broke, there was the sea before them and there was Pharaoh and his soldiers behind them. And his companions said to him: {Truly we are overtaken} (Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:61). And what was Moses' stand? He said, with complete confidence and tranquillity: {No indeed! Truly my Lord is with me; He will guide me} (Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:62).

And his people witnessed that when God commanded him to take that thin, slender staff and strike the sea with it, and the sea split apart and became like great mountains; and Moses and his people travelled a dry road in the sea, {fearing no overtaking and no dread} (Sūrat Ṭā Hā 20:77). And Pharaoh followed him with his soldiers until, when they were in the middle of the sea, it surged and overflowed and swallowed them and left of them no remnant.

We find this stand repeated also with Muhammad, God bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions, when Nuaym ibn Masud came to them and said: {The people have gathered against you, so fear them — and it increased them in faith and they said: God is sufficient for us, and an excellent Guardian is He. So they returned with a blessing from God and a bounty; no evil touched them, and they followed the good pleasure of God} (Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:173–174).

The one who reaches the station of reliance upon God, glorified and exalted, and complete confidence in Him, is the mighty one whose might suffers no drawing back, because he knows that his might is from the abiding, everlasting might of God.

God has written this might for those who travel this road; it is not particular to certain persons. So no one can say: "Those stands belonged to those prophets and have come to an end." Rather this state is repeated and continuing: every legally responsible believer who believes in God and is content with Him as Lord — the same situation is repeated with him when the pressures accumulate and the people of this world gather their forces and muster them. If he is one who has might through God, he will say what Noah said: {So decide upon your affair, you and your partners, then let not your affair be a cause of distress to you; then carry out your decision against me and give me no respite} (Sūrat Yūnus 10:71). And he will say what Hud said: {Truly I have relied upon God, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but He holds it by its forelock. Truly my Lord is upon a straight path} (Sūrat Hūd 11:56).

And by that he will see that all souls are in the hand of God, glorified and exalted — when He wills He takes them, and when He wills He sends them back: {God takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died in their sleep; then He withholds those upon which He has decreed death and sends back the others until an appointed term} (Sūrat al-Zumar 39:42).

And he knows that hearts likewise are between two of the fingers of the Merciful, He turns them about as He wills. So the one whom he dreads and whose enmity he remembers — is he not abased before the authority of God, exalted be He? Is he not in the grasp of His right hand?

The Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, said to the two envoys of Chosroes when they came: "Did Chosroes send you?" They said: "Yes." He said: "His son killed him last night." The one whom these two envoys fear, and for whose authority and command they travel a vast distance — his own son killed him last night.

Whoever knows that God, glorified and exalted, has the whole affair in His hand and to Him the whole affair returns cannot be deceived by anything of the affairs of this perishing world, knowing that it is a test and a setting-over from God, glorified and exalted. For people in it, within God's dominion, are but as ants and kinds of insects. All of them are sent; so if God, glorified and exalted, sends a harm, it must inevitably arrive, and abasing oneself before it does not save; and if He does not send it, it cannot harm nor arrive in any way whatever: {Whatever mercy God opens to people, none can withhold it; and whatever He withholds, none can release it after Him} (Sūrat Fāṭir 35:2); {And if God touches you with harm, there is none to remove it but He; and if He touches you with good, He has power over all things} (Sūrat al-Anʿām 6:17); {And if God touches you with harm, there is none to remove it but He; and if He wills good for you, there is none to turn back His bounty. He causes it to reach whomever He wills of His servants} (Sūrat Yūnus 10:107).

The believer who takes his might from God, glorified and exalted, and from His way, looks at what happens in the earth as people look at what happens in the sky. For God, glorified and exalted, made clear that He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whomever He wills; and made clear that He sends in the rain what He sends in it of kinds of harm, and that He strikes with it whomever He wills and turns it away from whomever He wills. The flash of His lightning almost takes away the sight; God turns about the night and the day — truly in that is a lesson for those who have eyes.

If a person looks at the doings of the people of this world and what is in it, and knows that it is decreed and written, and that the pens have been lifted and the pages have dried concerning what is to be, he cannot fear a created being, because he knows that what befalls him is from God and cannot be turned away from him, and that what God has not decreed should befall him cannot reach him in any way whatever.

*From which of my two days shall I flee from death — the day that is not decreed, or the day that is decreed? The day that is not decreed I do not dread; and when it is decreed, wariness does not save.*

This requires of a person complete might through God, glorified and exalted, and connection with Him in the manner that pleases Him.

God, glorified and exalted, has made easy for a person the paths of good and established the proof against him by all these matters we have mentioned. But many people are distracted from those paths by other matters and by the byways of the road, so that he supposes that some created being can benefit him or harm him, and that if he draws near to him and becomes one of those attached to him, or of those of his court, or of those who are welcomed with him at occasions, or who appear with him in the media, he will attain by that might and standing.

This is the utmost error in conception. For God, exalted be He, says: {O people, a parable is struck, so listen to it. Truly those you call upon besides God will never create a fly, even if they gathered together for it; and if the fly should snatch away something from them, they could not rescue it from it. Feeble is the seeker and the sought} (Sūrat al-Ḥajj 22:73).

For that reason, a man of the people of Yemen — an envoy came to him from an angry king and said: "The king summons you to attend at once," and the envoy was insisting on haste. So he said to him: "Will you permit me a question, my lord?" He said: "Go ahead." He said: "This king who summons me to attend — does he go to the privy? Does he need water?" He said: "How can you ask such questions?" He said: "One who goes to the privy and needs water cannot be feared; and if we hurry and come at the appointed time, he may be occupied with one of these matters."

And likewise is the case with regard to the side of covetousness. A person must remember that provision is entirely in the hand of God, and that he attains of it only what has been written for him, in any case whatever. If he surrendered his dignity and his selfhood and consented to be one of the attendants and servants, he could not be provided with more than what was written for him in any case whatever; it cannot increase by so much as what an ant carries of provision, however much he attends and serves.

If a person remembers that, he knows that the One who deserves that a person should desire what is with Him and covet what is with Him is the Sovereign, the Judge, alone. For that reason al-Makkudi, may God have mercy on him, says:

*When a need arises for me in my time, and its purposes have become obscure to me, I stand at the door of God the stand of a humble petitioner and say: My God, I am one who seeks You. And you will not see me standing at the door of one whose servant says: My master is asleep today.*

For one who sleeps and falls ill cannot be coveted from, because if he were able to benefit he would have benefited himself and would not have needed another. Therefore might must be sought from God alone.

This might God has written for the believers — but not for every believer. Rather none of the believers attains it but one who has struggled against his own soul until he reaches the station of reliance upon God, glorified and exalted.

Many of the texts containing a promise, or a mention of one of the stations, which is ascribed to the believers, are not intended to apply to every believing man and woman. Rather it is attained only by the elect of the believers, who struggled against their own souls until they became upright upon the way of God. Those are the ones who deserve these medals and deserve this honouring from God. So those of the believers who do not attain this might — that does not mean that they are not believers, but it means that they are deficient in faith. For it is attained only by one who struggled against his own soul until he reaches the station of reliance, which is among the high stations in faith.

Khalid ibn al-Walid, may God be pleased with him, when God granted him victory at the campaign of Yarmuk, asked the Byzantines about the most harmful of their weapons, and they pointed to a poison that kills within the hour. So he said: "In the name of God, with whose name nothing in the earth or in the sky can cause harm; and He is the Hearing, the Knowing" — and he drank that poison. Then he said: "What is the most harmful thing after this poison?" They said: "The sun." So he sat out in the sun exposed, and the Byzantines were amazed.

For this poison — merely by smelling its odour, since it is volatile, a person dies; and the sun is the most harmful thing for one who has been poisoned. And Khalid drinks it and then sits in the sun, and is unaffected, and begins to judge between people in their disputes while sitting in the sun.

That was a cause of the acceptance of Islam by the captives. Whenever a captive accepted Islam and bore witness that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, Khalid would rise to him and untie his bonds and say: "You are now our brother; what is binding upon us is binding upon you" — and he would teach him what he needed of the rulings of his religion. And he would not finish teaching one captive before another captive was ready for Islam, and Khalid would go forward to him and untie his bonds.

Those people witnessed this might in those men and they were a lofty example to them, and that was the cause of their believing and accepting Islam.

This state which happened to Khalid ibn al-Walid, when he relied upon God, glorified and exalted, and sought refuge in Him — it cannot be objected against him that he did a forbidden thing contrary to the revealed law when he drank the poison, and that it is not lawful for a person to drink it — because that is according to the state of the person himself. If he was one of certainty, who had reached the degree of certainty that nothing harms him except what has been written for him, and was certain that he had heard this report from the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, and that whoever says "In the name of God, with whose name nothing in the earth or in the sky can cause harm; and He is the Hearing, the Knowing" three times, nothing harms him — and he was certain of that — then at that point there is allowed to him what is not allowed to another; and that is not realised for him [otherwise].

Then those who came after them, of those who travelled this road, showed this level of might through God, glorified and exalted, even in the harshest and most constricted situations.

Thus the Imam Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn al-Tayyib al-Baqillani — the caliph of the Muslims sent him to the king of the Byzantines to negotiate. In the days of Islam's might the envoys were the great scholars: when a scholar among the great scholars of the Muslims became renowned, the caliph would choose him as an envoy to negotiate in the name of the Muslims — as Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan did when he sent Amir al-Shabi to the Byzantines, and as the king of the Banu al-Abbas did when he likewise sent Abu Bakr al-Baqillani to them.

It was the custom of the Byzantines that everyone who entered the king's court had to bow before him. So they said: "How shall we make this scholar bow?" And their men of judgement came and thought about it, and they made a step in the door through which one entered the king's assembly, and left of the door's height only as much as a man could enter through bowing.

When al-Baqillani came he saw this device and understood it, so he turned his back to them and came in crawling backwards. And the king put his hand over his face out of shame at this sight, and they knew that they had not attained from him what they sought. And when he saw his face he rose to him in admiration and esteem and seated him with him upon his couch, and began to introduce to him those in his assembly: "This one on your right is the Pope, the head of the Church, the head of religion among us."

So he turned to the Pope and greeted him and said: "How are your wife and your children?" And everyone in the assembly clamoured and said: "We hold him far above what you are asking about." So he said: "Glory be to God! You do not hold the One who created him far above it, yet you hold him far above it? You claim for God a consort and a child, and you hold the Pope far above being so?" So he silenced them all and went out of their assembly.

The like of this was repeated with a shaykh among the shaykhs of Damascus who was in the Umayyad Mosque at the time when Ibrahim Pasha, the ruler of Egypt, entered — when he came in with his armies and overran Damascus, he asked: "Who is left of the notables of Damascus who has not received me?" It was said: "Such-and-such a shaykh — there he is, sitting in the mosque of the Banu Umayyah teaching students of knowledge." So he said: "Come, let us go to him."

So the king went out to him with his soldiers, the Turks bearing arms, until they entered the mosque and stood over the shaykh. And he did not change his seated posture, nor cut off his teaching, nor was his face affected by looking at them. When they entered, one of the students said to him: "This is the king, and his soldiers have entered the mosque." He said: "It has been related to us that looking at the faces of the oppressors hardens the heart" — and he commanded the students not to look at them with their eyes, lest their hearts harden.

So the king came humbly until he sat before him, and the shaykh continued his teaching while the king listened to the teaching until he finished the lesson. Then he greeted him and he returned his greeting. Then the shaykh stretched out his leg in the king's face — and this is something the Turks regard as very grave, and the non-Arabs consider it the utmost in humiliation and contempt. So the king rose and sent him a great sum of money; and when the messenger came to him carrying the money he said: "Go back to him and tell him: one who stretches out his leg does not stretch out his hand."

This might is attained only by those who are truthful with God, glorified and exalted.

Then, one who reaches this level of reliance upon God, glorified and exalted, and of confidence in Him, cannot be affected by worldly calamities. Even if he is degraded with kinds of harm and tried with kinds of affliction, he will remain mighty and steadfast through all of that.

Thus Ahmad ibn Hanbal remained in prison for eighteen years, with fetters on his hands and his feet, and was beaten with whips so that he would say a single word — and he accepted nothing of that in any way whatever. He relates of himself that he said: "I was carried to Baghdad with the chains — chains of iron — on my hands and my feet, and an aged shaykh of the people of al-Mahallah (a place in Baghdad) came in to me and said: 'Ahmad, you are today a head among the people, so be patient upon the truth, for the people are with you'" — that is, followers of yours. Ahmad said: "As God wills." So he knew that this shaykh was a making-firm from God, whom He had sent to make him firm by him; and he stood firm upon that and continued upon it until the trial was lifted.

And likewise the case with what happened to a number of those who went before, when they were made to suffer degradation and were harmed with kinds of harm — they would not draw back from their principles nor surrender in any way whatever.

Thus Habib ibn Zayd, may God be pleased with him, when he came to Musaylimah the Liar, he began saying to him: "Do you bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of God?" and he would say: "I bear witness." Then he would say: "Do you bear witness that I am the Messenger of God?" and he would say: "I am deaf." So he would cut off a limb from him, then repeat the question to him, then cut off another limb from him — until he cut him limb from limb, while he stood firm upon his word, unaffected.

And likewise the woman of the ditch, who was carrying a suckling infant in the cradle. When she stood over the fire she remembered the state of this infant and that she would fall with him into that terrifying fire, and she hesitated a little. And the infant in the cradle said to her: "Mother, the fire of this world is easier than the fire of the hereafter." So she threw herself with him into that fire. And God sent down concerning that a Qur'an, in Sūrat al-Burūj.

Whoever grasps this station — the pressures he faces become of little weight to him, and he cannot be enticed by any enticement whatever. For the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, when the people of Mecca offered to make him king over them and informed Abu Talib of that, said to him: "Uncle, if they were to place the sun in my right hand and the moon in my left, on condition that I abandon something of what has come to me from my Lord, I would not do any of that."

And Sad ibn Abi Waqqas, when his mother went on hunger strike and abstained from food until she nearly died, so that he would turn back from his religion, whispered in her ear and said: "Mother, if you had a hundred souls, and they went out one soul after another, on condition that I turn back from my religion, I would not turn back. So live or die."

Those people knew that what is with God, glorified and exalted, is the abiding and everlasting, and that what is other than it is of the matters that are cut off, which none is eager for but the weak.

Thus Musab ibn Umayr — there was not in Mecca a young man of greater refinement than he. When he passed along a road, the scent of perfume was known in that road from his passing along it. His mother used to buy him a garment every month, and he would not wear it in any other month, and she used to indulge him with kinds of what he needed.

Then when he accepted Islam she charged strong men with him and confined him between four walls, and they used to beat him morning and evening and harm him with kinds of harm; and he was deprived of everything, being only in iron and fetters, so that he would turn back from the religion — and he did not accept.

And when the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, chose him as an envoy — the first envoy in Islam — to Medina, he went out with nothing upon him but a cloak of his and his sword. And the condition remained thus for three years after the emigration: he was killed on the day of Uhud in the third year of the emigration, having nothing but his sword and a cloak upon him. If we covered his head with it his feet showed, and if we covered his feet his head showed. So the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, ordered us to cover his head and to put some idhkhir grass over his feet. So he had nothing of his reward hastened to him — but he knew, and held fast; he knew the truth, and it held fast to him.

Likewise, those of the later generations who travelled this road were also exposed to much harm and pressure so that they would turn back from what they were upon — and that increased them only in steadfastness and in continuance upon it and in might through God, glorified and exalted, even in the most critical and severe situations.

Thus Sayyid [ibn] Qutb, may God have mercy on him: at his execution a man of the scholars of al-Azhar came to him wishing to prompt him with the testimony of faith, and said to him: "Say: there is no god but God." He said: "I am dying upon it, and you are living by it — you make your living from it." For this one who casts this word upon him knows nothing of it but its wording, and takes pounds for it by which he lives; while he is being killed in its cause.

And likewise, when they asked him, as he was being brought to the gallows, to write an apology — even a single line — so that he might be pardoned, he said: "This finger which I raise in the testimony of faith is for God, glorified and exalted; I cannot contradict that with it."

This stand recurs often in this community. Those who have tasted the flavour of faith and have grasped that might is obtained by connection with God, glorified and exalted, cannot be affected by any pressure whatever, nor be drawn along behind any enemy of the enemies of God, glorified and exalted.

The learned Mawlud ibn Ahmad al-Jawad, may God have mercy on him, said:

*I entrust to the Preserver, the Keeper of what is entrusted, the Guardian, my religion and myself and my brothers and my wealth; and I ask the Most High to grant me success and to set right my deeds and my words. I am the weak one, and that weakness is pitied by my Lord the Strong — so weakness was the stronger for me. He is never abased, never abased, who has might through God; and how often the mighty one has been abased through uncles on the father's side and on the mother's. How often we have seen one abased after his might — one whose might was through patrons or through wealth. When my hand wins the allegiance of God, then, O created being, be an enemy or an ally as you will.*

Allegiance to God, glorified and exalted, requires of a person that he know that none benefits and none harms but He alone, and that he travel the way He has approved for him, and that he know that He is with him wherever he is. For God, glorified and exalted, said to Moses and Aaron: {Truly I am with you both, hearing and seeing} (Sūrat Ṭā Hā 20:46). And He addressed the believers with His words: {And He is with you wherever you are} (Sūrat al-Ḥadīd 57:4). And He, exalted be He, said: {There is no secret conference of three but He is their fourth, nor of five but He is their sixth, nor of fewer than that nor more but He is with them} (Sūrat al-Mujādalah 58:7).

Whoever wants the companionship of God, glorified and exalted, and His help and His establishment, must be with God in all his states, and must know that in his public state he is as in his private state, and that his turning towards God in ease ought to be like his turning towards Him in adversity. Come to know God in ease and He will know you in hardship. For the one who comes to know God in ease is the one who attains such stands as these and such honouring as this, with the great steadfastness at the time of friction and trials.

But as for the one who knows God, glorified and exalted, only at the time of hardship — his state is the state of those who associate partners with God, who, when harm touches them at sea, those they call upon vanish except God; and then they raise their voices in supplication, calling upon God, like the state of Pharaoh when the drowning overtook him and he said: {I believe that there is no god but the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of those who submit. Now? And you disobeyed before, and you were among the corrupters} (Sūrat Yūnus 10:90–91).

So there must be a coming to know God in ease, so that a person may attain that making-firm and that help in hardship. A person must be with God, glorified and exalted, in the state of blessing: if He bestows blessing upon him, he is with Him in the state of blessing, so that this blessing does not lead him astray and he does not transgress on account of it.

The servant who knows God only in the state of his illness and in the state of his weakness and in the state of his destitution and poverty, and resorts to God only at those times, cannot attain that relief which is attained by the truthful affirmers of God's oneness, who came to know God in ease so that He came to know them in hardship.

It is upon each one of us to remember that God, glorified and exalted, has placed upon this road many obstacles, and that they lie ahead awaiting him: what does not befall him today will befall him tomorrow. Accordingly he considers his steadfastness before these shocks.

For the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, said to the woman whom he found weeping at the grave of a child of hers: "Servant of God, be conscious of God and be patient." She said: "Away from me — for you have not been afflicted with the like of my affliction." It was said to her: "Woe to you, it is the Messenger of God." So she came to excuse herself to him and said: "Messenger of God, by God, I did not recognise you." He said: "Patience is only at the first shock."

So a person must keep present that patience is at the first shock. For that reason Ali, may God be pleased with him, when he was asked about courage — it was said: "What is courage?" — said: "Patience for an hour." That is, that a person should habituate himself to patience in the places of encounter.

And he must know that those calamities have befallen one better than he, and that if they befall him there is no harm in it. Did not Noah, peace be upon him, bear patiently with calamities and trials and harm for a thousand years less fifty? Is he not nobler in the sight of God than we are? Was not Abraham cast into the fire? Did not Muhammad, God bless him and grant him peace, meet with a great deal of kinds of harm? For Uqbah ibn Abi Muayt put the afterbirth upon his back between his shoulders while he was prostrating to his Lord; and he and Abu Jahl came and put a rope around his neck and pulled at him while he was praying, until Abu Bakr came and struck them with his shoulders, saying: "Would you kill a man for saying: My Lord is God?"

He met with a great deal of kinds of harm. Therefore we must know that we are travelling his road and that we must inevitably meet with some of what he met with. For God, exalted be He, said: {You shall certainly be tried in your properties and your selves, and you shall certainly hear from those who were given the Book before you and from those who associate partners with God much harm. And if you are patient and God-conscious, that is among the matters requiring resolve} (Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:186).

Therefore do not expect that the affairs of religion will remain like this — a person sitting comfortably in a mosque listening to a lecture, for example, and by this being among the helpers of God to this extent only. Rather you must remember the words of God, exalted be He: {So their Lord answered them: I do not let the work of any worker among you go to waste, male or female; you are from one another. So those who emigrated and were driven from their homes and were harmed in My cause and fought and were killed — I shall surely efface their evil deeds from them} — these are the conditions of the Lord of might — {and I shall surely admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow, as a reward from God; and God — with Him is the best of reward} (Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:195).

And He, exalted be He, said: {Alif Lām Mīm. Do people reckon that they will be left to say "We believe" and not be tried? We tried those before them, and God will surely know those who are truthful and will surely know the liars} (Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt 29:1–3).

So a person must be conscious that ahead of him are many trials and afflictions upon the road of truth, and that he is prepared for patience and endurance upon this road, as the wise man said:

*The man of understanding pictures his calamities in his mind before they descend; so if they descend suddenly they do not alarm him, because of the picture that was in his soul. But the man of ignorance feels safe in his days and forgets the fallen who have gone before; so if the turns of time overwhelm him with some of their calamities, he wails aloud.*

So a person must keep present the road of those who travelled this road before him, and that it is not lined with roses but is full of thorns. This this-worldly path upon which we travel is a representation of the path of the hereafter, which is finer than a hair and sharper than a sword, and upon which are hooks like the thorns of the saʿdān plant; people differ upon it according to their deeds. And whoever is more firm upon this this-worldly path is more firm upon the path of the hereafter.

Therefore it is upon us all to be eager to improve our relationship with God, glorified and exalted, and connection with Him and reliance upon Him and coming to know Him in ease; and to keep present that ahead of us are many trials upon this road; and to habituate ourselves to patience when calamities come; and to know that they are not in the hands of created beings but are in the hand of God — for the created being cannot lift a harm nor send it down; that is all in the hand of God, glorified and exalted, and by His command.

These truths which we believe in must be embodied in practice in our deeds. It is not enough that you say "I believe in the decree, its good and its evil; I believe that the pens have been lifted and the pages have dried," until you arrive at the result of believing in the decree. For God mentioned the decree in one verse and mentioned its result in the verse after it. He, exalted be He, said: {No calamity befalls in the earth or in yourselves but that it is in a Book before We bring it into being. Truly that is easy for God} — this is the decree — then He said: {so that you may not grieve over what has escaped you, nor exult over what He has given you} (Sūrat al-Ḥadīd 57:22–23). This is the result of believing in the decree, namely: "so that you may not grieve over what has escaped you" — and grief is sorrow — "nor exult over what He has given you."

So if a person actually realises this result, he is a believer in the decree, its good and its evil. But if he does not realise it, he will be like those who clamour with a statement whose reality and meaning they do not grasp, like one who is prompted with words and repeats them like a parrot.

It is upon us to know that those who attained this might by connection with God, glorified and exalted, in the great situations were the friends of God in the state of ease, and were among those obedient to His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. So God, glorified and exalted, realised for them what was promised, because He knew truthfulness from their hearts.

Therefore we must be truthful with God, glorified and exalted, in our whole affair, and must know that might through His religion is the real might. For the lineages and ancestries by which people take might are all cut off and have no meaning. People are from Adam, and Adam is from dust. Whoever takes might from a lineage in this worldly life — it is perishing and short, and that lineage will be cut off the moment the trumpet is blown: {Then, when the trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship between them on that day, nor will they ask after one another. Then those whose scales are heavy — those are the ones who prosper; and those whose scales are light — those are the ones who have lost their own souls, abiding in Hell for ever. The Fire will scorch their faces and they will be grimacing in it} (Sūrat al-Muʾminūn 23:101–104).

Boasting of worldly lineages and offices and ancestries has no meaning, for it is cut off and vanishes in the swiftest of times. For that reason look at those who are buried in this earth: in the adjoining plots you find the grave of the king and the grave of the commoner, the grave of the rich man and the grave of the poor man, the grave of the scholar and the grave of the ignorant man — and they are equal; all their graves are equal. Their reports were cut off the moment they were laid in the dust.

So we know that the grave is either a meadow among the meadows of the Garden or a pit among the pits of the Fire; and that cannot be known through its outward appearance or what we see above it. The grave over which mosaic is laid and upon which ornaments are placed or trees are planted, and the grave that has no mark upon it, are the same. So the lesson is not in the surface of the earth, but in the person within it — and his destiny there has been shown to him: {And there will appear to them from God what they had not reckoned upon} (Sūrat al-Zumar 39:47).

If a person grasps this, he knows that what people take might from of the affairs of this world has no effect in might, and knows that the real might is when God whitens his face so that he walks in light a journey of five hundred years, and gives him his book in his right hand before his face, and brings him across the path like flashing lightning, and places between him and his enemies a wall with a gate, within which is mercy and outside which, before it, is punishment — and then after that admits him to the gardens of bliss. This is the great triumph; and if a person attains it, by God, what he missed of the affairs of this world does no harm to him.

Whoever's face is whitened on the day when faces are whitened and faces are blackened, and takes his book in his right hand — by God, people's contempt for him in this world does him no harm, nor that he lived poor, or lived weak, or despised in this worldly life; none of that harms him.

I have explained to you that a person's lifespans are five. His first lifespan is the lifespan of the particles, when God wiped the back of Adam and brought forth from him his offspring and said: "Am I not your Lord?" and they said: "Yes." This lifespan is long, and the obligation in it is only the affirmation of God's oneness: "Am I not your Lord?" {Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan — truly he is to you a manifest enemy — and that you should worship Me? This is a straight path} (Sūrat Yā Sīn 36:60–61).

The second lifespan is a person's lifespan upon this earth, and it is the shortest of his lifespans, and it is the lifespan of legal responsibility.

The third lifespan is his lifespan in the interspace, in the belly of the earth, and it is long if compared with his lifespan above it.

The fourth lifespan is his lifespan upon the plain at the gathering: {And truly a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count} (Sūrat al-Ḥajj 22:47).

And the fifth lifespan is the eternal, everlasting lifespan, in a Garden or in a Fire.

So if a person knows that the duration of his abasement and his humiliation is the duration of this short worldly lifespan — and that even everything in it does not last, even the abasement in it does not last, and the bliss in it does not last — if a person grasps that, this becomes light upon him against what he hopes for with God, glorified and exalted, at the standing, when God places the just upon pulpits of light at the right hand of the Merciful — and both His hands are right hands — and likewise when they enter the Garden and the Maker, glorified and exalted, manifests Himself to them from above them and says: {"Peace" — a word from a Merciful Lord} (Sūrat Yā Sīn 36:58). At that point there is no harm upon them, even if they met with whatever kinds of harm they met with in this worldly life.

It is upon us all to take our might from belonging to God, glorified and exalted, and from attachment to His religion, and to free ourselves from everything Satan casts upon us of the kinds of false takings-of-might.

Taking might from the tribe is of the affair of the age of ignorance. The people of that age used to take might from their tribes, and the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Whoever among you claims kinship with the claim of the age of ignorance, bid him bite his father's member, and do not use a euphemism."

And they likewise used to take might from wealth and children, and He, glorified and exalted, said: {Leave Me with him whom I created alone, and gave him extended wealth and sons present with him, and prepared for him a full preparation; then he covets that I should increase. No indeed! He has been obstinate towards Our signs. I shall burden him with a steep ascent} (Sūrat al-Muddaththir 74:11–17) — and it is the ascent of a mountain among the mountains of the Fire, and "I shall burden him" — he is made to carry it upon his back on the Day of Resurrection; we ask God for safety and well-being — "I shall burden him with a steep ascent."

Therefore we must free ourselves from all the shackles of the age of ignorance. We must know that excellence among people is only by God-consciousness. Whoever fears God, mighty and majestic, and fears His punishment and guards against His anger, is the one who deserves might. And whoever does not fear God, there is no good in him — the beasts are better than he, for at least they are not legally responsible and so are not disobedient. And one than whom a beast is better certainly cannot take might; one whose donkey is better than he — how should he take might?

It is upon us to realise that the real values are what God has set out in His Book, for He said: {O people, We created you from a male and a female, and made you into peoples and tribes that you might know one another. Truly the noblest of you in the sight of God is the most God-conscious of you} (Sūrat al-Ḥujurāt 49:13).

So whoever is more God-conscious is the nobler and the more elevated in the sight of God, and we do not care about his lineage. For all people will flee from their fathers and their mothers and their spouses and their children on the Day of Resurrection: {On the day a man flees from his brother, and his mother and his father, and his wife and his sons — for every man among them on that day there is a concern that occupies him} (Sūrat ʿAbasa 80:34–37); {The criminal will wish that he might ransom himself from the punishment of that day by his sons, and his wife and his brother, and his kin who sheltered him, and whoever is in the earth all together — then it would save him} (Sūrat al-Maʿārij 70:11–14).

If a person knows that, all the matters by which people take might in this worldly life become light upon him — and likewise if he remembers the swiftness of their vanishing.

How many a man mighty in this world have we seen who became one pushed away at the doors! Do you not recall that many of the presidents and kings who had effective command, and whom people dreaded in the offices, are today turned back from the offices that were subordinate to them, in which they used to appoint whomever they wished and dismiss whomever they wished — and here they are today pushed away from them at the doors?

Do you not see that those who were rich — and especially those who used to take wealth from other than its lawful source — many of them have been prevented from that and have derived no benefit at all from it; rather many of them have lived poor, owning nothing, after having been rich?

Whoever knows that realises that nothing of what people take might from of the affairs of this world remains, and that permanence belongs to the abiding righteous deeds, as God, exalted be He, said: {And the abiding righteous deeds are better with your Lord in reward and better in hope} (Sūrat al-Kahf 18:46); {And the abiding righteous deeds are better with your Lord in reward and better in outcome} (Sūrat Maryam 19:76).

The abiding righteous deeds are the good deeds which God, glorified and exalted, accepts. They are the abiding ones which do not pass away as the affairs of this world pass away; and they are righteous [and sound] because they do not fall ill and are not struck by calamities — they are full and complete with God, glorified and exalted.

We ask God, glorified and exalted, by His beautiful names and His lofty attributes, to give us might through His religion and to give His religion might through us, and to make us a delight to the eye of His Prophet Muhammad, God bless him and grant him peace, and to make us hold fast to his sunnah when his community is corrupted. And may God bless and grant peace to our master Muhammad and to his family and his Companions all together.

flags.arabic: لا يمكن أن يعترض عليه بأنه فعل أمرا محرما مخالفا للشرع حين شرب السم ولا يحل للإنسان أن يشربه، لأن ذلك بحسب حال الإنسان نفسه، فإن كان موقنا … فحينئذ يسوغ له ما لا يسوغ لغيره، ولا يتحقق له ذلك
flags.context: Immediately after the account of Khalid ibn al-Walid drinking poison at Yarmuk.
options: Render the general prohibition and the exception exactly as given, marking the closing clause as unclear, as done here
Read the closing clause as 'and that is not realised for anyone else'
Withhold the passage from display pending confirmation
flags.note: THE MOST DANGEROUS PASSAGE IN THIS SLICE IF MISREAD. The Sheikh states plainly that drinking poison is a forbidden act contrary to the revealed law and that IT IS NOT LAWFUL for a person to drink it — and then says that Khalid is not to be objected against, because the matter depends on the individual's own state, and that for one who has reached the station of certainty 'there is allowed to him what is not allowed to another'. The general prohibition must be unmistakable in any English display; an excerpt that carried only the exception could be read as licence to take poison, with lethal consequences. The final clause, 'wa-lā yataḥaqqaqu lahu dhālik', is grammatically unclear as printed: it may mean 'and that is not realised for him [i.e. for anyone else]', or a word may have dropped out. It has been rendered with a bracketed marker rather than resolved. A reviewer must settle this clause before publication, because it is the clause that closes the exception off.

flags.arabic: فهذا سيد بن قطب رحمه الله عند قتله … قال: أنا أموت عليها، وأنت تحيى بها تتعيش بها … إن هذه الإصبع التي أرفعها في التشهد لله سبحانه وتعالى، لا يمكن أن أخالف بها ذلك
flags.context: The last of the examples of steadfastness under pressure.
options: Translate the account exactly as given, as done here
Render it without the invocation of mercy upon Sayyid Qutb
flags.note: EDITORIAL REVIEW REQUIRED. The Sheikh cites Sayyid Qutb, executed in Egypt in 1966, as an exemplar of steadfastness, invokes God's mercy upon him, and relates his retort to the Azhar scholar and his refusal to write an apology. Sayyid Qutb is among the most contested figures in modern Islamic thought, and a favourable citation of him carries significant reputational and, in some jurisdictions, legal weight. The Sheikh endorses only his steadfastness at execution; he does not here endorse any of Qutb's doctrines, and no such endorsement may be read into the English. Note also that the source writes 'Sayyid ibn Qutb'; the name is Sayyid Qutb, and the intrusive 'ibn' is a source error, preserved in body_ar and marked in the English with brackets. Publication decisions belong to Ummah Collective and the Sheikh's office.

flags.arabic: من تعزى عليكم بعزاء الجاهلية فأعضوه بهن أبيه ولا تكنوا
flags.context: On taking might from tribal belonging.
options: bid him bite his father's member, and do not use a euphemism
bid him bite his father's private part, and do not soften it
rebuke him in the coarsest terms, without euphemism
flags.note: A genuine translation dilemma that cannot be resolved without a decision from the Sheikh's office. This is a transmitted prophetic report whose own operative instruction is 'do not use a euphemism' (wa-lā taknū) — that is, the coarse word is to be said plainly and not veiled. Rendering it with a euphemism in English therefore contradicts the content of the report itself, while rendering it plainly produces obscene English on a public page. The English here takes the middle course of a plain but non-obscene noun and keeps the instruction visible, which is a compromise and should be recognised as one. Style guide 6 forbids softening a text to suit an audience, so the decision about the register of the English belongs to Ummah Collective and the Sheikh's office, not to the translator.

flags.arabic: فهذا أحمد بن حنبل مكث في السجن ثماني عشرة سنة
flags.context: On Ahmad ibn Hanbal's endurance under the inquisition.
options: Report the figure exactly as the Sheikh gives it, as done here
Note in the body that the historical period of imprisonment was shorter
flags.note: The Sheikh gives eighteen years of imprisonment in chains. The same figure is given in ID 479/494 of this slice, so it is his settled way of putting it and not a transcription slip. The standard biographical accounts give a much shorter period of actual imprisonment, with the wider miḥnah extending over some fifteen to eighteen years across three caliphates; the Sheikh appears to be counting the duration of the trial rather than of the confinement. Style guide 6 forbids adding a qualification he did not give, so the figure stands as he states it and the point is raised here for the reviewer.

flags.arabic: وقد بينت لكم أن أعمار الإنسان خمسة
flags.context: Introducing the scheme of the five lifespans in the closing third of the lecture.
options: Render as a back-reference to an earlier lecture, as done here
Render as though the scheme were being introduced for the first time
flags.note: 'I have explained to you' is an explicit back-reference to material the Sheikh taught on another occasion which is NOT contained in this record. The scheme as given here — the lifespan of the particles, of this world, of the interspace, of the gathering, and the eternal one — is therefore a summary of a fuller treatment elsewhere in the corpus. A display should not present it as a self-contained teaching, and a reviewer may be able to identify the parent lecture and link it.

flags.arabic: «أي يومي من الموت أفر…» / «إذا عرضت لي في زماني حاجة…» / «أستودع الحافظ المستودع الوالي…» / «يمثل ذو اللب في لبه…»
flags.context: Four passages of verse distributed through the lecture.
options: Render as prose in italics and keep the Arabic in the bilingual pane, as done here
Reproduce the source's double-asterisk hemistich separators
flags.note: Four separate quotations of verse, with hemistichs separated in the source by double asterisks. Style guide 4: rendered as prose in italics, with no rhymed English attempted. Two poets are named — al-Makkudi, and the Mauritanian scholar Mawlud ibn Ahmad al-Jawad, whose lines on weakness as strength are the most substantial of the four; the other two are given as 'the wise man' and unattributed. The Jawad lines contain one plainly corrupt reading: 'bi-aʿmām wa-akhwāl' where the metre and sense suggest a different phrase, and 'bi-l-amwāl' is printed 'bi-l-amwāl' without its alif. Neither has been corrected.

flags.arabic: عن يمين الرحمن، وكلتا يديه يمين … فيتجلى لهم الباري سبحانه وتعالى من فوقهم
flags.context: The description of the standing and of the entry into the Garden.
options: Render the attribute statements literally, as done here
Render them with an interpretive gloss
flags.note: Creedal statements of divine attributes, rendered literally without interpretation (taʾwīl) and without adding a doctrinal gloss the Sheikh did not give. Style guide 8: these are propositions about God, not rulings about acts, and the five-rulings mapping does not touch them. The clause 'and both His hands are right hands' is itself part of the transmitted wording and has been kept. Compare the affirmation of God's aboveness in ID 479/494, which is the same theological position stated polemically.

flags.arabic: لكن ليس ذلك لكل مؤمن، بل لا ينالها من المؤمنين إلا من جاهد نفسه حتى يصل إلى مقام التوكل … فالذين لا ينالون هذه العزة من الذين آمنوا ليس معنى ذلك أنهم غير مؤمنين لكن معنى ذلك أنهم ناقصو الإيمان
flags.context: The hinge of the lecture's argument about who attains might.
options: Preserve the qualification in full, as done here
Render only the claim that might belongs to the believers
flags.note: An important qualification that must not be lost in excerpting. The Sheikh restricts the promise of might to the elect among the believers who have reached the station of reliance — and then explicitly guards against the takfīrī reading, stating that those who do not attain it are NOT thereby outside faith but are deficient in it. Given the takfīr language elsewhere in this slice (ID 479/494), this guard is significant and has been preserved in full.

flags.arabic: ألا تذكرون أن كثيرا من الرؤساء والملوك الذين كان لهم الأمر النافذ … وهاهم اليوم يدفعون عنها على الأبواب
flags.context: Near the close of the lecture.
options: Translate exactly as given, as done here
Render the passage in more general terms
flags.note: A pointed passage on deposed presidents and kings and on those who amassed wealth unlawfully and lost it, delivered in a specific setting in or before 2010. The Sheikh names no person, country or government anywhere in the lecture, and no name has been supplied. Compare the similar passage on deposed rulers in hiding in ID 477. Translated faithfully; a reviewer should weigh the local political charge before publication.

flags.arabic: وهي صالحة لأنها لا تمرض ولا تصاب بالمصائب
options: righteous [and sound]
righteous
sound
flags.note: A play on the two senses of ṣāliḥ that does not survive into English on its own: the Sheikh glosses 'al-ṣāliḥāt' not only as 'righteous' but as 'sound' in the sense of being free of defect — 'they do not fall ill and are not struck by calamities'. The English marks the second sense in brackets so the gloss is intelligible. A reviewer may prefer a different solution.

This is a complete lecture transcript (dars), not a sermon: it opens with the basmalah and 'ammā baʿd' and closes with a supplication and the prayer upon the Prophet, with no two-part structure and no sermon formulae. It is typed as a transcript accordingly. Note that, unlike the transcripts at IDs 478 and 488, it does not open with the greeting of peace.
This record uses '(ṣ)' throughout as an abbreviation for the prayer upon the Prophet, as IDs 478 and 491 do. The English expands it; body_ar preserves the abbreviation.

CRITICAL FOR DISPLAY. The passage on Khalid ibn al-Walid and the poison states a general prohibition and then an exception tied to a personal station of certainty. Displayed or excerpted without the prohibition, it could be read as licence to ingest poison. The record should not be excerpted at that point, and the closing clause of the passage is grammatically unresolved in the source and flagged.

EDITORIAL REVIEW REQUIRED. Besides the poison passage, the record cites Sayyid Qutb approvingly as an exemplar of steadfastness; quotes a prophetic report whose own instruction forbids euphemism and whose plain rendering is obscene; and closes with pointed remarks about deposed rulers and the unlawfully rich. All are translated faithfully and none is softened, as style guide 6 requires. Style guide 12: publication decisions belong to Ummah Collective and the Sheikh's office.

The lecture's argument is a single sustained one and should be displayed whole: that might (ʿizzah) belongs to God alone, so that it is attained only by connection with Him and not by wealth, office, lineage or proximity to power; and that the station at which it is attained is the station of reliance (tawakkul), which is reached by struggle against the self and is not the portion of every believer. The historical examples — Abraham, Moses, the Companions at al-Hudaybiyah, Khalid, al-Baqillani, the shaykh of Damascus, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Habib ibn Zayd, the woman of the ditch, Musab ibn Umayr, Sayyid Qutb — are all illustrations of that one thesis, in rough chronological order.

Several narrations here are given without a named collection and without a grading, including the account of Khalid and the poison, the embassy of al-Baqillani and the story of the shaykh of Damascus, which are historical reports rather than prophetic ones. Style guide 4 forbids adding a grading the Sheikh did not give, so nothing has been supplied.
